title: A Value Over Time: The Chart That Lies About Steady Signals

questions.question: A battery reading is steady to within two microvolts. Drawn on an axis fitted to it, what does the chart show?
options: Violent oscillation filling the whole height, because the scale expanded until the last digit of the reading filled it
A flat line, since the signal is flat
Nothing, since the span is too small to draw
A slow drift
questions.explanation: Measured: more than fifteen rows of twenty. A change of one part in ten million is drawn exactly as large as a change of one volt, and people respond by filtering a signal that was never noisy.

questions.question: Why is padding the range by a fraction not a fix for that?
options: A fraction of nearly nothing is nearly nothing, so the span stays collapsed
Padding is applied before the range is computed
Padding only affects the time axis
It is a fix, but a slow one
questions.explanation: Padding and widening a flat axis are different decisions and belong in different functions, so a reader can see which one a caller asked for.

questions.question: A rolling window keeps the last five hundred samples. What is wrong with that?
options: Five hundred samples is fifty seconds at ten hertz and half a second at a thousand, so the x axis means something different on every run
Five hundred is too few for a chart
It uses unbounded memory
Nothing, if the rate is known
questions.explanation: Drop by age, which is the policy, and keep a capacity as a separate guard, which is what stops a faster than expected signal growing the buffer without limit.

questions.question: Why draw the time axis from the window rather than from the samples that arrived?
options: A gap in the data is then drawn as a gap, instead of being spread evenly and hidden
It is faster to compute
The samples may be out of order
The window is easier to label
questions.explanation: A missing four seconds is often the most important thing on the chart. Passing the mapping a time rather than an index is also what makes the wrong version hard to write.

questions.question: How should a minimum span be chosen?
options: From what counts as a change in the signal, which the chart cannot know and its author can
As a fixed fraction of the reading
As the smallest value the sensor can resolve
Large enough that no signal ever fills the chart
questions.explanation: For a battery, a tenth of a volt is a change worth seeing and a microvolt is not. A minimum so large that a genuine event disappears has traded one lie for another.

questions.question: Which pair of checks keeps an axis rule honest?
options: A steady signal must not fill the chart, and a real change must still be visible on the same rule
The span must be positive, and the range must contain every sample
The chart must redraw at a fixed rate, and the axis must be labelled
The range must be padded, and the padding must be symmetric
questions.explanation: Either one alone is easy to satisfy wrongly. Together they pin the rule between the two ways it can be wrong.
